question: What first drew you to fashion design as something you wanted to study seriously?
lookingFor: A specific, personal moment or process that shows real engagement, not just a love of shopping or clothes.

bullets: Name a concrete moment, project, or person that sparked it
Show the shift from liking clothes to wanting to make them
Connect it to what you've done since to pursue it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started altering my own clothes at fourteen because nothing in shops fit the way I wanted, and taking in a jacket myself was the first time I realised construction was a puzzle I actually enjoyed solving. That turned into making pieces for friends, then a small capsule collection for a school show using only secondhand fabric. It stopped being about wearing clothes and became about making decisions on paper and cloth, which is why I want to study it properly now.

commonMistakes: Saying only 'I've always loved fashion' with nothing concrete
Describing themselves purely as a consumer of trends
Giving an answer that could apply to any creative subject
followUps: What's the first garment you ever made, and what did you learn from it?

question: Why do you want to study fashion design here rather than at another institution?
lookingFor: Specific knowledge of the course's structure, facilities, or faculty, tied to the applicant's own gaps or goals.

bullets: Reference a specific module, studio, tutor, or industry link on this course
Explain what that gives them that they don't already have
Avoid generic praise that could apply to any fashion school
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at your second-year brief that pairs students with a local textile mill, because I've only ever worked with fabric I bought off the roll and I want to understand how cloth is actually made before I keep designing with it. I also want the pattern-cutting studio time your course gives compared to others I researched, since that's the technical skill I'm weakest in right now. I'm not looking for a general art degree, I want the specific discipline of turning ideas into wearable garments, and this course is structured around exactly that.

commonMistakes: Citing university ranking or reputation alone
Vague praise that fits any fashion program
Not knowing any specifics about the actual course structure
followUps: What's a gap in your current skills you're hoping this course will close?

question: Talk us through one piece in your portfolio and how it developed from idea to final outcome.
lookingFor: Evidence of a real design process, including research, iteration, and decisions made along the way, not just the finished look.

bullets: Describe the starting point or research that sparked the idea
Explain at least one decision that changed during development
Reflect honestly on what worked and what they'd improve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My final piece started from photographs I took of rust patterns on an old gate near my house, which became the basis for a print I hand-dyed onto cotton. My first toile used a fitted bodice, but it fought with the print, so I reworked it into a looser silhouette that let the pattern actually breathe across the fabric. Looking back, I'd spend longer on the hem finish, since it's the one detail that still looks slightly rushed under close inspection.

commonMistakes: Describing only the finished garment with no process
Claiming everything went perfectly with no iteration
Being unable to explain a single design decision behind the piece
followUps: What would you change if you made that piece again today?

question: Which designer or design house influences your work, and what specifically do you take from them?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific reference point that reveals real research and taste, not a name-drop.

bullets: Name a designer and a specific body of work, not just a brand name
Identify a concrete element of technique, silhouette, or philosophy they draw from
Connect it to their own design instincts, not just admiration
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to Issey Miyake's Pleats Please work, particularly how the pleating does the shaping instead of a seam or dart. What I take from it isn't the pleating technique itself but the idea that construction can be the decoration, that you don't need to add embellishment if the structure already tells a story. My own sketches lean toward that now, trying to get fabric manipulation to do work that most people would solve with print.

commonMistakes: Naming a designer with no specific reason why
Only referencing celebrity or red carpet fashion
Copying the designer's aesthetic wholesale with no personal angle
followUps: Where does your own work diverge from theirs?

question: What's the difference between a fashion designer and a stylist, and which are you actually interested in?
lookingFor: Clear understanding that design is about creating garments while styling is about curating and combining existing pieces.

bullets: Define designing as creating original garments from concept, pattern, and construction
Define styling as selecting and combining existing pieces for a look or shoot
State clearly which one they're applying for and why
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A designer creates the garment itself, from the first sketch through pattern cutting and construction, deciding the fabric, silhouette, and detail before anything exists. A stylist works with garments that already exist, choosing and combining them to build a look for a shoot, show, or client. I'm interested in design specifically because I want to be responsible for the object itself, not just how it's presented afterward, which is why the making side of your course matters most to me.

commonMistakes: Using the two terms interchangeably
Only describing styling because it sounds more glamorous
Unable to say clearly which path they actually want
followUps: Have you done any work that overlaps with styling, and how was it different?

subtopic: Design process from concept to garment
question: Walk us through your typical process when you're developing a new design, from first idea to finished garment.
lookingFor: A structured, personal process showing research, sketching, fabric decisions, and testing rather than an ad hoc description.

bullets: Start with where ideas come from, research or reference gathering
Move through sketching and fabric or silhouette decisions
Mention testing or toiling before final construction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start with a mood board of images that have nothing to do with fashion, often architecture or landscape, because that keeps me from copying what already exists in clothing. From there I do rough thumbnail sketches until one silhouette feels right, then I choose fabric based on how it needs to move or hold shape. Before cutting anything final I always make a calico toile first, because that's where I catch problems with fit or proportion while it's still cheap to fix.

commonMistakes: Describing a process with no research stage at all
Skipping straight from sketch to finished garment with no testing
Giving a vague answer that isn't actually their own process
followUps: What do you do when a toile reveals the idea doesn't work?

question: Fashion is often criticised as one of the most polluting industries. What responsibility do you think a designer has around sustainability?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, realistic position that acknowledges the industry's impact without either dismissing it or offering only slogans.

bullets: Acknowledge the scale of the industry's environmental impact honestly
Identify a specific, realistic lever a designer controls, such as fabric choice or garment longevity
Avoid empty buzzwords, show it in something they've actually tried
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think designers can't fix the whole industry alone, but we do control real decisions, like choosing fabrics that last and biodegrade over ones that shed microplastics, or designing garments meant to be repaired rather than replaced. For my last project I deliberately used deadstock fabric from a local supplier instead of ordering new, partly to test whether limited materials would actually make me a better problem solver, and it did. I don't think sustainability is a trend to bolt onto a collection, I think it has to shape the decisions from the very first sketch.

commonMistakes: Using vague buzzwords with no concrete example
Claiming the issue is entirely the consumer's responsibility
Dismissing sustainability as irrelevant to creative work
followUps: What's a sustainable material or technique you'd want to learn more about?

question: What's your view on fast fashion, and how does it affect the kind of designer you want to become?
lookingFor: A nuanced, non-preachy view that connects the applicant's own design values to the debate, not just condemnation.

bullets: Show understanding of why fast fashion exists, including price and access
State a personal position without being dismissive of people who rely on it
Connect it to how they want to design differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand why fast fashion exists, it makes trend-driven clothes affordable for people who'd otherwise be priced out, and I don't think it's fair to just blame consumers for that. What worries me more is the design philosophy behind it, garments made to be worn a handful of times and discarded, which pushes against everything I want from construction. I want to design pieces built to be altered and kept for years, which means thinking about durability and timelessness from the first sketch rather than chasing a two-week trend cycle.

commonMistakes: A purely moralising answer with no nuance
Ignoring the economic reasons fast fashion exists
Not connecting the critique back to their own design values
followUps: Do you think slow fashion can ever be made affordable at scale?

question: What's the difference between how a fabric like silk chiffon and a fabric like denim behave, and why does that matter when designing?
lookingFor: Practical understanding that fabric weight, drape, and structure dictate silhouette choices, not just aesthetic preference.

bullets: Describe drape versus structure in concrete physical terms
Explain how each fabric suits different silhouettes or garment types
Show this is learned from handling fabric, not just theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Silk chiffon is lightweight and fluid, it drapes and moves with the body, so it suits soft gathers, flowing skirts, or bias-cut pieces where you want movement rather than structure. Denim is heavy and holds its own shape, which is why it works for tailored, structured pieces like jackets or fitted trousers that need to keep a defined silhouette. If I designed a fitted bodice in chiffon it would collapse without heavy interfacing, and if I tried soft gathers in denim they'd just look bulky, so the fabric has to be chosen alongside the silhouette, not after it.

commonMistakes: Describing fabrics only by look, not by how they behave when worn
Being unable to name a garment type suited to each
Confusing fibre content with weave or weight
followUps: Name a fabric you've struggled to work with and why.

question: How do you approach choosing a colour palette for a collection?
lookingFor: Basic understanding of colour relationships and how palette choices serve mood, cohesion, or story, not random preference.

bullets: Reference a basic colour relationship, complementary, analogous, or monochrome
Explain how the palette needs to work across a whole collection, not one piece
Connect the palette choice to mood or concept
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start from the mood I want the collection to have, then build a small palette around that, often analogous colours so pieces feel cohesive when worn together rather than fighting each other. For my last project based on autumn hedgerows, I picked rust, moss, and a muted cream as the core three and let one accent colour appear sparingly across the range to tie it together. I try to test the palette on fabric swatches early, because colours read very differently on paper than they do on cloth.

commonMistakes: Choosing colours purely because they personally like them
No understanding of how colour needs to work across a full collection
Confusing colour theory terms without being able to apply them
followUps: Has a colour ever looked different on fabric than you expected, and what did you do?

question: Can you explain the difference between an A-line silhouette and a sheath silhouette?
lookingFor: Clear, accurate technical knowledge of two basic silhouette types and where each is typically used.

bullets: Describe the A-line as fitted at the top and flaring toward the hem
Describe the sheath as fitted close to the body throughout
Give an example garment or context for each
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An A-line silhouette is fitted through the shoulders or bust and then gradually widens toward the hem, so it looks like the letter A, which is flattering because it skims rather than clings. A sheath silhouette follows the body's shape closely from top to bottom with minimal flare, so it needs more precise fitting because there's nowhere for the eye to look but the actual line of the body. I tend to use A-line shapes when I want movement in a garment and sheath shapes when I want the fabric or print itself to be the focus.

commonMistakes: Confusing the two silhouettes or their names
Describing silhouette in terms of print or colour instead of shape
Unable to give an example of either in use
followUps: Which silhouette do you find hardest to design well, and why?

question: What's the difference between draping and flat pattern cutting, and which do you prefer working with?
lookingFor: Understanding of both core pattern-making methods and a genuine, reasoned preference based on experience.

bullets: Describe draping as working fabric directly on a stand or body
Describe flat pattern cutting as working from measurements on paper
State a preference grounded in actual hands-on experience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Draping is working fabric directly onto a mannequin or a person, pinning and shaping it in three dimensions until you find the line you want, which is how a lot of asymmetric or fluid designs get developed. Flat pattern cutting starts on paper, using measurements and blocks to build a pattern mathematically before it's ever cut in fabric, which gives you more precision and repeatability. I lean toward draping because I think better in three dimensions than on paper, though I know flat cutting is the skill I need to get more disciplined about for tailored pieces.

commonMistakes: Being unable to describe either method accurately
Claiming to prefer one with no real hands-on basis
Treating the two as interchangeable rather than distinct skills
followUps: Describe a garment where draping would be the wrong choice.

question: Tell us about a time a tutor or peer criticised your design work harshly. How did you respond?
lookingFor: Genuine openness to critique in a creative field, with evidence they used feedback rather than just defended the work.

bullets: Describe the specific critique honestly, not a softened version
Show the initial emotional reaction without dwelling on it
Explain the concrete change made as a result
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A visiting tutor told me my final collection sketches all looked the same silhouette repeated in different fabrics, which stung because I'd thought I was showing range. My first instinct was to defend it, but I sat with the feedback overnight and realised she was right, I'd been safe rather than exploratory. I went back and pushed three of the five looks into much more experimental shapes, and the collection was stronger for it, even though it meant scrapping work I'd already spent weeks on.

commonMistakes: Describing a critique so mild it doesn't show real growth
Getting defensive in the retelling rather than reflective
No concrete change made after the feedback
followUps: Has feedback ever been wrong, in your view? How did you handle disagreeing with it?

question: Is there a period or moment in fashion history that particularly interests you, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with fashion history beyond famous names, showing curiosity about context and cultural change.

bullets: Name a specific period, movement, or moment, not just 'vintage'
Explain the social or cultural context that shaped it
Connect it to something in their own thinking or work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn to the shift after the Second World War, when Dior's New Look reintroduced full skirts and structured waists right after years of fabric rationing had forced minimal, utilitarian design. What interests me is how directly the silhouette responded to scarcity, extravagance became a kind of statement precisely because it had been impossible. It's made me think more carefully about how constraints, whether fabric shortages or a small budget, actually shape design decisions rather than just limiting them.

commonMistakes: Naming a vague era like 'the 90s' with no specific reasoning
Reciting facts with no personal connection to the interest
Confusing historical periods or getting basic facts wrong
followUps: How does that period show up, even subtly, in your own design work?

question: How do you see technology like CAD software or 3D printing fitting into fashion design, and how comfortable are you with it?
lookingFor: Realistic, current understanding of digital tools in the design process, plus honesty about their own skill level.

bullets: Name a specific technology and its actual use in the design workflow
Give an honest self-assessment of current skill, not overclaiming
Show it complements rather than replaces hand skills
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've used basic CAD software to lay out repeat prints and to visualise a colourway across a whole collection before committing fabric, which saves a lot of wasted material. I'm still a beginner at it though, most of my strength is in hand sketching and physical pattern work, and I know that's a gap I want this course to close. I don't think digital tools replace draping or sewing, but they're useful for planning and communicating ideas quickly before you commit real fabric to them.

commonMistakes: Overclaiming expertise they don't actually have
Dismissing digital tools as irrelevant to 'real' design
No concrete example of having used any such tool
followUps: What's one digital skill you specifically want to learn on this course?

question: Fashion often draws on cultural dress and traditions for inspiration. How do you think about the line between inspiration and appropriation?
lookingFor: Nuanced ethical reasoning that takes the issue seriously without either dismissing it or refusing to engage with cultural influence at all.

bullets: Acknowledge that fashion has a real history of taking without credit or understanding
Propose a practical way to engage respectfully, such as research, collaboration, or attribution
Avoid both defensiveness and empty caution that avoids the topic entirely
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the line usually comes down to whether you're actually engaging with the meaning behind something or just lifting its surface look because it's visually interesting. If I wanted to reference a specific textile tradition, I'd want to research where it comes from, understand what it means to the people who make it, and credit it properly rather than presenting it as my own invention. I'd also rather collaborate with makers from that tradition where possible than design in isolation and hope I got it right, because respect has to show up in the process, not just a caption.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the concern as oversensitivity
Refusing to engage with any cultural reference out of fear
Giving a rehearsed answer with no real reasoning behind it
followUps: Can you think of an example, from any designer, that got this balance right or wrong?

question: How do you keep up with what's happening in fashion right now, and how much do trends influence your own work?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with current fashion sources, plus a thoughtful view on trend-following versus personal voice.

bullets: Name specific, real sources they actually follow
Show awareness of at least one current shift or discussion in fashion
Explain how they balance trend awareness with their own point of view
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I follow a handful of independent designers on social media rather than just the big houses, and I read trend forecasting reports when my school library gets them, because I want to understand the industry side, not just the pretty pictures. Right now I'm noticing a lot of interest in quiet, minimal tailoring as a reaction against a few years of maximalism. I take trends as information about where the conversation is, but I try not to let them dictate my own design decisions, otherwise everything I make would look dated within a season.

commonMistakes: Naming only Instagram or celebrities with no substance
Claiming to ignore trends entirely, which reads as naive
Being unable to name any current shift in the industry
followUps: What's a current trend you actively dislike, and why?

question: What sewing or construction skills do you already have, and where do you feel least confident?
lookingFor: Honest, specific self-assessment of technical skill level, showing they've actually made garments, not just imagined them.

bullets: List specific skills they've actually practiced, not general claims
Name a genuine weak spot honestly
Show awareness of why that weak spot matters
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm confident with basic garment construction on a machine, setting in sleeves, sewing darts, and simple zip insertion, and I've done a bit of hand finishing like blind hemming. Where I'm weakest is tailoring, I've never properly worked with canvas interfacing or padstitching a lapel, and my one attempt at a jacket came out stiff in the wrong places. I know that's a real gap because so much structured design relies on those techniques, so it's one of the first things I want to get proper instruction in.

commonMistakes: Claiming broad expertise with no specific detail
Refusing to name any actual weakness
Confusing hand sewing with machine construction terms
followUps: What's the most technically difficult thing you've successfully made?

question: Most fashion education and industry sample sizes are built around one body type. How would you approach designing for a wider range of bodies?
lookingFor: Awareness that standard sizing excludes most bodies, plus a genuine, practical idea for approaching fit differently, not just good intentions.

bullets: Acknowledge the real limitation of standard sample sizing
Propose a concrete practical approach, such as grading, adaptable design, or testing on varied fit models
Avoid treating inclusivity as an afterthought or marketing point
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the industry habit of designing on one sample size and grading up or down afterward is exactly why fit often breaks down outside that size, because proportions don't scale evenly. If I were designing a range, I'd want to fit-test on more than one body from the start, not just adjust a single pattern mathematically, and build in features like adjustable waistbands or wrap closures that can genuinely flex across different shapes. I don't think this is a separate 'inclusive line' problem, I think it should just be how fit is approached from the first toile.

commonMistakes: Treating inclusive sizing as a marketing add-on rather than a design problem
Vague good intentions with no practical mechanism
Denying that standard sizing is a real limitation
followUps: Have you ever designed or fitted a garment on a body different from your own? What did you learn?

question: Do you see yourself eventually starting your own label, or working within an established design house? What appeals to each?
lookingFor: Realistic understanding of both paths and their trade-offs, not a naive assumption that starting a label is simple or glamorous.

bullets: Show understanding of what each path actually involves day to day
Give an honest current leaning while staying open
Reflect realistic awareness of the business demands of running a label
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I lean toward working within an established house first, partly because I want to learn how production, sourcing, and budgets actually work at scale before I'd trust myself to run those decisions alone. Starting a label appeals to me long term because I like the idea of full creative control, but I've read enough about the failure rate of small labels to know it's not just about talent, it's cash flow, suppliers, and things I have zero experience with yet. I'd rather build that knowledge inside a company first than learn it the hard way with my own money.

commonMistakes: Assuming starting a label is purely a creative decision with no business risk
Giving no real preference or reasoning at all
Dismissing working for an established house as lacking ambition
followUps: What's one business skill you think designers underrate?

question: Tell us about a time you had to design within a tight brief or constraint you didn't choose. How did you handle it?
lookingFor: Evidence they can work creatively within limits rather than only when fully free, an essential skill for any design course or career.

bullets: Describe a real constraint, material, budget, theme, or deadline
Show how the limitation shaped rather than blocked the creative decision
Reflect on what they learned about working within limits
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For a school project we were given a brief to design using only fabric already in the classroom store, which was mostly plain cotton in a handful of colours, nothing I'd have chosen myself. Instead of fighting the limitation I leaned into it, using pleating and layering to create texture and interest that the plain fabric alone couldn't give. It ended up teaching me more about manipulating fabric than any project where I'd had free choice, because the constraint forced me to solve the problem with technique instead of just picking a more interesting material.

commonMistakes: Describing only projects with total creative freedom
Treating the constraint as purely a limitation with nothing gained
Vague description with no specific brief or outcome
followUps: What's a constraint you'd actually find creatively useful going forward?

question: How do you communicate a design idea before it becomes a garment, sketching, flats, mood boards? Walk us through your approach.
lookingFor: Practical familiarity with how designers communicate ideas visually before construction, and why each tool serves a different purpose.

bullets: Name at least two distinct tools, such as loose sketches, technical flats, or mood boards
Explain what each is actually used for in the process
Show this is habitual practice, not a one-off exercise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start with loose, quick sketches just to get a silhouette idea out of my head onto paper, without worrying about accuracy. Once I've settled on a direction, I draw a proper technical flat with exact proportions and stitch lines, because that's what I'd actually hand to someone cutting a pattern. I also keep a mood board running throughout, less for the silhouette and more to keep the fabric, colour, and overall feeling consistent across a whole collection.

commonMistakes: Naming only one tool with no understanding of the others
Confusing a technical flat with a fashion illustration
Describing this as something they've never actually done
followUps: What's the hardest thing to communicate through a flat sketch alone?

question: You clearly have a strong creative and artistic sensibility. Why fashion design specifically, rather than fine art or textiles?
lookingFor: A clear articulation of what makes fashion distinct, the body, function, and wearability, rather than treating it as interchangeable with fine art.

bullets: Identify what's unique to fashion, such as designing for a moving body or real-world function
Show they've considered and ruled out adjacent fields deliberately
Ground the answer in their own creative instincts, not just a preference for practicality
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I love that fashion has to work on a body that moves, breathes, and lives in the world, which is a constraint fine art doesn't have and one I find genuinely interesting to solve rather than limiting. I did consider textiles, since I love pattern and surface, but I realised what excites me most is the whole garment, silhouette and construction as much as surface decoration. Fashion is where those things all have to come together and actually function, and that combination is what I want to spend years getting better at.

commonMistakes: Treating fashion and fine art as basically interchangeable
Dismissing fine art or textiles as lesser rather than different
Giving an answer with no real reflection on the distinction
followUps: Where do you think fine art and fashion design genuinely overlap?

question: Fashion courses and the industry both run on tight, unmoving deadlines, a show date doesn't shift. Tell us about a time you had to finish a piece under real time pressure.
lookingFor: Evidence of practical time management and composure under a fixed deadline, with an honest account of what actually happened.

bullets: Describe a genuine deadline crunch, not a comfortable one
Explain the specific decisions made to get it finished, cutting scope, prioritising, asking for help
Reflect honestly on what they'd do differently next time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Two days before a school exhibition, I realised the hand-embroidered panel I'd planned for my final piece would take three times longer than I'd budgeted. I made the call to finish only the front panel by hand and simplify the back with a simpler stitch, rather than risk missing the deadline entirely with an unfinished garment. It wasn't the piece I'd originally envisioned, but it taught me to build in a buffer and to test how long hand techniques actually take before committing to them so close to a deadline.

commonMistakes: Describing a deadline they had plenty of time for
Claiming everything went smoothly with no real pressure
No specific decision made to manage the crunch
followUps: How do you plan your time differently now, having learned that?

question: If you had to describe your design philosophy or point of view in a couple of sentences, what would it be, and how would we see it in your work?
lookingFor: A distinct, self-aware creative identity backed by evidence in their actual work, not a borrowed or generic mission statement.

bullets: State a genuine, specific point of view, not a vague mission statement
Explain why that view matters to them personally
Point to concrete evidence of it showing up in real work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn to imperfection as a design principle, visible seams, uneven dye, asymmetry, because I think the handmade quality of a garment should be visible rather than hidden. That comes from growing up watching my grandmother mend and remake clothes rather than replace them, so imperfection always read to me as evidence of care, not failure. You can see it in my portfolio piece with the exposed raw-edge seams, which I left deliberately unfinished instead of overlocking them away.

commonMistakes: Reciting a vague, generic mission statement with no real content
A philosophy with no evidence of it in their actual work
Copying language that sounds impressive but isn't genuinely theirs
followUps: Has that philosophy ever conflicted with a brief or expectation you had to meet anyway?
